questions.c-45: The autocorrelation function is the correlation of a weakly stationary series with itself at a lag, and the partial autocorrelation is the correlation of the two endpoints after linear adjustment for the observations in between.
questions.c-46: An autoregressive order counts lagged observations in the linear predictor, a moving-average order counts lagged innovations, and an ARMA model uses both.
questions.c-50: ARCH models let a series' conditional variance depend on recent squared shocks, and GARCH models also let it depend on recent conditional variances.
questions.c-26: The Bradley–Terry model gives each competitor a positive strength and takes the probability that one beats the other, with no ties, to be that competitor's share of the two strengths.
questions.c-24: A nominal response has unordered categories, an ordinal response has ordered categories, and a baseline-category logit compares each other category's probability with a chosen baseline category.
questions.c-36: Responses can be independent given a random effect and still be correlated in the marginal distribution obtained by integrating that effect out.
questions.c-37: A logistic mixed-model coefficient is a log-odds change at a fixed random effect, while a population-average coefficient describes the marginal mean after those effects are averaged out.
questions.c-31: A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic polynomial with continuous value, slope and curvature, and a knot is an abscissa where two of those pieces meet.
questions.c-08: A marginal likelihood is the probability of the data after the model's parameters are integrated out, and a Bayes factor is the ratio of two models' marginal likelihoods.
questions.c-19: Fisher scoring updates a parameter with the score and the expected Fisher information, and in a generalised linear model that update is iteratively reweighted least squares.
questions.c-34: A fixed effect is an unknown constant in the mean, and a random effect is a group-level draw from a distribution shared across groups.
questions.c-13: A full conditional is the distribution of one unknown given the data and all the other unknowns, and a Gibbs sampler draws each unknown in turn from its full conditional.
questions.c-33: A generalised additive model replaces linear terms by smooth functions of covariates, and the effective degrees of freedom summarise how flexible a fitted smooth is.
questions.c-38: Generalised estimating equations estimate the parameters of a marginal mean model for correlated responses, using a working correlation rather than a full likelihood.
questions.c-49: The shapes of the autocorrelation and partial autocorrelation functions suggest autoregressive and moving-average orders, and the residual autocorrelation is then checked for correlation the fit has left behind.
questions.c-01: After the data are observed, the likelihood is a function of the parameter, the prior describes parameter uncertainty before those data, and the posterior describes it afterwards.
questions.c-17: A link maps the mean of a response onto the linear predictor, the inverse link maps the linear predictor back to the mean, and a canonical link matches the exponential family's natural parameter.
questions.c-21: In a Poisson regression with a log link and no interactions, the exponential of a coefficient is the multiplicative change in the mean when that covariate increases by one unit and the others stay fixed.
questions.c-07: A maximum a posteriori estimate maximises the posterior density, whereas the Bayes estimate under squared-error loss is the posterior mean.
questions.c-12: The Markov property says the future depends on the past only through the present state, and an invariant distribution is unchanged by one step of the transition kernel.
questions.c-14: Metropolis–Hastings can use an unnormalised target because the normalising constant cancels in the acceptance ratio, and the proposal densities cancel when the proposal is symmetric.
questions.c-11: A Monte Carlo estimate averages a function of draws from the target distribution, and Monte Carlo error is the sampling variability of that average.
questions.c-22: A negative-binomial count model has a variance that can exceed its mean, while a Poisson model forces the variance to equal the mean.
questions.c-09: Complete pooling uses one shared parameter, no pooling estimates each group on its own, and partial pooling shrinks group estimates toward a common distribution.
questions.c-23: Gamma and inverse-Gaussian generalised linear models are for positive continuous responses, with variance proportional to the square of the mean and to its cube, respectively.
questions.c-05: A posterior prediction averages the sampling model over the posterior of the parameters, while a plug-in prediction uses one fitted parameter value and omits that parameter uncertainty.
questions.c-42: A stochastic process is a collection of random variables indexed by time or space, and an observed time series is one realisation of such a process.
questions.c-25: The proportional-odds assumption uses one covariate coefficient for every cumulative logit, so the odds ratio for that covariate is the same at each cutpoint.
questions.c-27: A quasilikelihood model specifies how the mean depends on the covariates and how the variance depends on the mean, without specifying a full response distribution.
questions.c-35: A random intercept shifts a group's baseline and a random slope changes a covariate's effect across groups, and in a generalised linear mixed model both enter the conditional linear predictor.
questions.c-32: Penalising the integrated square of a function's second derivative discourages curvature, and a larger penalty weight pulls the fit toward a straight line.
questions.c-40: The generalised-estimating-equation sandwich covariance stays consistent when the working correlation is wrong, but it does not repair an incorrect mean model.
questions.c-18: The score vector is the gradient of the log-likelihood, and the expected Fisher information is the variance of that score under the model.
questions.c-03: A statistic is sufficient for a parameter when the conditional distribution of the sample given the statistic does not depend on that parameter.
questions.c-06: A 95 percent credible interval has posterior probability 0.95 of containing the parameter, while a 95 percent confidence interval comes from a procedure that covers the parameter in 95 percent of repeated samples.
questions.c-47: A unit root at one is an autoregressive root on the unit circle, and in an ARIMA model the orders count autoregressive terms, differences, and moving-average terms.
questions.c-41: Vector-response regression records several outcomes on the same unit, and generalised estimating equations can give each outcome its own marginal link and variance while allowing association within the unit.
